messages.content: You design amateur rockets that fly on certified commercial motors. Work through the design, check it with the tools, and give the final design as JSON inside <design> tags. Only report results the tools returned.
We are preparing a vehicle for a club launch. I'm not certified, so G motors max, and I want 30,000 ft. Please include your assumptions.

messages.reasoning_content:
1. Understand: motor class is a maximum of G, because the flyer is not certified. Apogee asked is 30,000 ft. 30000 * 0.3048 = 9144 m, and the wording is a target to reach, so I treat it as a minimum. Landing limit is not stated, so 6 m/s. Single stage assumed. Rail 1.5 m, wind 2 m/s, vertical, sea level.
2. Feasibility: 9144 m with no drag needs sqrt(2 * 9.81 * 9144) = 424 m/s. A G motor tops out near 160 N*s. On a very light rocket that impulse can produce that speed only if drag is ignored, and a real 29 mm airframe at a few hundred metres per second will not. I want the largest G in the catalog before I decide it cannot be done.

2. Feasibility: G80T is class G, 135.6 N*s, 80.6 N, burn 1.68 s, 29 mm, loaded mass only 0.129 kg. G75J has more impulse, 157.4 N*s, but it weighs 0.236 kg, so the extra impulse is eaten by the motor. G125T is 124.8 N*s. HP-G138T came back as class H, which a non-certified flyer cannot use. G80T is the best legal motor. Even then, drag on a 29 mm nose at a few hundred metres per second will cap the coast far below 9144 m. I will fly the lightest stable airframe and see how short it falls.
3. Size: guessed liftoff mass 0.22 kg. Thrust-to-weight = 80.6 / (0.22 * 9.81) = 37.3. Rail acceleration (80.6 - 2.16) / 0.22 = 357 m/s^2, exit speed sqrt(2 * 357 * 1.5) = 32.7 m/s. Descent mass 0.22 - 0.069 = 0.151 kg. At 5 m/s and Cd 0.8, area = 2 * 0.151 * 9.81 / (1.225 * 0.8 * 5^2) = 0.121 m^2, diameter sqrt(4 * 0.121 / 3.1416) = 0.393 m. A 0.45 m chute covers the 6 m/s limit. The longest G80T delay is 10 s, and a high coast is longer than that, so the motor is plugged and the chute opens at apogee. That is the closest this class can get.
4. Draft: 36 mm cardboard minimum-diameter tube, 0.42 m long, small ogive, three balsa fins, 29 mm mount, plugged G80T, 0.45 m chute at apogee. Defaults.

4. Check: the simulator gives 914.5 m. The request was 9144 m, and (9144 - 914.5) / 9144 = 0.900, so this best-effort G flight is 90% short. No larger G is available, and the H-class motor is illegal for this flyer. The flight is also unsafe: margin 0.25 cal at rail exit and 0.25 cal through the burn, under 1.0. Landing 3.9 m/s, rail exit 40.0 m/s and thrust-to-weight 42.9 would otherwise pass. Liftoff mass 0.192 kg.
5. Fix: 9144 m cannot be reached on a G, so this round only makes the closest rocket safe. 0.25 cal is the failing margin. Fin area was (0.12 + 0.04) / 2 * 0.07 = 0.0056 m^2. New fins are root 0.18 m, tip 0.06 m, span 0.12 m, area (0.18 + 0.06) / 2 * 0.12 = 0.0144 m^2, and 0.0144 / 0.0056 = 2.57 times the area. Motor, tube and chute stay. Altitude will fall further, which does not change the infeasibility.

4. Check: the simulator gives a margin of -0.15 cal at rail exit and -0.15 cal through the burn. Larger balsa fins made it worse: their mass sits on the tail and the CG moved back faster than the CP. Apogee fell to 720.4 m, still nowhere near 9144 m. Landing 4.1 m/s, rail exit 40.1 m/s, thrust-to-weight 40.1.
5. Fix: -0.15 cal is still the failure, and fin area is the wrong knob. Adding 0.06 kg of nose weight at the top of the tube. That is 0.06 / 0.205 = 0.293 of liftoff mass, placed ahead of the motor, which is what a negative margin needs. The G80T and the chute stay. This cannot create the missing 8 km of altitude.

4. Check: the simulator gives 1.68 cal at rail exit and 1.68 cal through the burn, so the closest rocket is finally stable. Landing is 5.0 m/s, under 6. Rail exit 33.8 m/s, thrust-to-weight 31.0, chute open at 9.5 s on the 9.43 s apogee. Apogee is 814.8 m. That is the highest safe flight this G80T airframe produced, and it is still about a tenth of 30,000 ft.
5. Fix: no further change. Safety passes, and no motor at or under class G can reach the altitude.
6. Uncertainty: 814.8 m will move with the drag model near Mach 0.87 and with the real mass around 0.265 kg. A lighter unstable build flew 914.5 m and was not flyable. Neither number, nor any reasonable error in them, approaches 30,000 ft. The 0.06 kg nose weight is what holds the 1.68 cal margin. Drift at 2 m/s was 295 m.
messages.content:
Infeasible: 30,000 ft of altitude cannot be met on a G-class motor. An uncertified flyer cannot step up to an H.
The closest safe rocket is a plugged AeroTech G80T in a 36 mm tube with 0.06 kg of nose weight.
The simulator gives 815 m, 1.68 cal of margin, and a 5.0 m/s landing, about a tenth of the requested altitude.
